name: Aaron Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me out, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say goes out with your name. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the rural district out of the Hollow Creek depot, so it's farm lines, long runs of wooden poles across fields and along back roads. A normal day, we might be swapping a cross-arm on a pole in a cow paddock, or clearing a line a tree's come down on. My dad did this same district for thirty-one years, and half the farmers still call me Ray's boy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people out here know you. You fix their power during calving season and they bring you coffee and a slice of cake. What wears me out is head office in the city changing how things are done every year, new forms, new apps, new rules from people who've never seen a farm line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: don't believe everything you hear from people selling something. Nobody out here was holding their breath. I'd say that at the pub and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. If nothing changes, I keep my job and I keep doing lines work the way my dad showed me. That's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep my head down, keep saving. I've got a bit put away and Granddad's twelve acres with a few head of cattle on it, so I'm all right. I'd maybe fix up the old farmhouse on the land, that's been the plan for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My phone does enough already. The company keeps trying to get us onto some job app, and I fill it in at the end of the day because they make me, but that's as far as I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything on your mind for the next few years, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the usual. The depot's small and every few years there's talk of closing it and running us out of the town depot an hour away. That'd mean more driving and less knowing the farms. But AI's got nothing to do with that.

say: I'd say **don't believe** everything from people selling something.
I'd say nobody **out here** was holding their breath.
think: I'd be **glad**, because nothing changes and I keep my job.
I'd keep doing the work **the way my dad** showed me.
do: Keep working, **keep saving** and keep my head down.
Fix up **the old farmhouse** on my granddad's twelve acres.
Keep a **few head of cattle** on the land as before.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I keep my job and I keep doing lines work the way my dad showed me.
fieldNote: Aaron's identity is tied to **family tradition** and a known community.
His one standing worry is the **small depot** being merged into a town depot.
Land and savings give him a **solid cushion** beyond his wage.

steps.text: Keep working the Hollow Creek farm district as usual
Put money into fixing up Granddad's old farmhouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that'll change, not ours, mostly at the pub. Somebody still has to climb out in the rain. But I'd also say it's the big companies chasing profit, cutting people to make their shares look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gets my depot closed. If a computer can plan all the jobs from the city, why keep a small depot out here? My job's fine but my life gets worse: longer drives, more strangers, more rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and I'd keep saving. If they closed Hollow Creek, I wouldn't move to the city, I'd drive the hour. I'd also talk to the older guys about going to management together, to make the case for keeping the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like watching the weather turn and knowing you can't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the depot closing become more likely in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More likely, yes. They'd say the computer can dispatch us from town just as well. And Maureen (who runs our depot office) would be the first to go, she's been there since my dad's day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you only fill in the app because they make you. What if the new tools got heavier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn the minimum, same as now. I'd get my cousin's kid to show me on a Sunday. But I won't be one of these guys chatting to their phone like it's a person.

say: I'd say **office jobs** will change, not ours.
I'd blame **big companies** cutting people to please shareholders.
I wouldn't post anything, but I'd say it at **the pub**.
think: It probably gets my **depot closed**, since a computer can plan jobs from the city.
My job's fine, but my life gets worse: **longer drives** and more strangers.
do: Drive **the extra hour** rather than move to the city.
Go to **management** with the older crew to keep the depot open.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching weather turn that you can't stop.
S1.quote: If a computer can plan all the jobs from the city, why keep a small depot out here?
fieldNote: Aaron fears **losing his community**, not his job.
He blames **profit-chasing** big companies rather than the technology.
His protest is local and personal: a **group visit** to management.

steps.text: Keep saving a fixed amount from every pay
Join older crew members to press management to keep the depot
Drive an hour to the town depot rather than move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in government needs to slow this down, and I don't normally want government doing anything. Two years is madness. I'd say it at church and at the pub, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. The planning side goes in 2028, so the depot's gone for sure. Then robots by 2031, when I'm 31, and lines work is the only thing I've trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could, starting now. I'd stop the farmhouse work and keep the money in the bank. I'd build up the cattle on Granddad's land, because whatever happens people will eat beef, and that's something I can do with my hands. And I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your district crew when the robots come in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farm lines are rough. Uneven ground, cattle, mud, trees everywhere. I reckon the robots would do the city first and get to us last, maybe a couple of years later. But they'd get to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got land and savings. Does that change how this feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I'd never go hungry, I've got a roof and a bit of land, but that's not the same as having work you're proud of. That's what I'd be losing.

say: I'd say **government** should slow this down, though I rarely want government involved.
I'd call two years **madness** at church and at the pub.
think: The **depot's gone** in 2028 once planning goes.
By **2031** robots arrive, and lines work is all I've trained for.
do: Save everything and **pause the farmhouse** work.
Build up **the cattle** on my granddad's land as a hands-on backup.
Write to our **member of parliament**, for the first time ever.
S2.quote: I'd never go hungry, I've got a roof and a bit of land, but that's not the same as having work you're proud of.
fieldNote: Aaron's fear is about **pride in work**, more than money.
He breaks with his usual views and asks **government to slow** the change.
His fallback is **cattle on family land**, which matches his preference for hands-on work.

steps.text: Pause the farmhouse renovation and bank the money
Grow the cattle herd on Granddad's twelve acres
Write to the local member of parliament asking to slow the rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so let's use it to protect the people who've given their lives to this work. Apprentices, old hands, the lot. I'd say it at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same answer, just later. Robots by 2034 means I'd be 35, and probably still on my own with a farmhouse half done. I'd worry about it, but I'd keep telling myself the farm lines are the last place they'll reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep saving. I'd finish the farmhouse, because that's a home whatever happens. And I'd grow the cattle slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd sleep better than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home. In the fast picture I'd stop building the farmhouse, but here I'd finish it, and that matters to me more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider training for anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a welding ticket, or something on farm machinery. Something hands-on. I'm not going to sit at a computer, that's not who I am.

say: I'd say we should use the time to **protect the people** who gave their lives to this work.
I'd include **apprentices and old hands** alike.
think: It's the **same answer, later**, with robots arriving when I'm 35.
I'd keep telling myself **farm lines** are the last place robots will reach.
do: **Finish the farmhouse**, because it's a home whatever happens.
feel: **Anxious**, but sleeping better than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: In the fast picture I'd stop building the farmhouse, but here I'd finish it, and that matters to me more than anything.
fieldNote: For Aaron, extra time means **finishing a home**, not changing careers.
He'd consider only **hands-on training**, such as welding or farm machinery.
He admits he'd rely on **hope** that rural lines come last.

steps.text: Finish renovating the farmhouse on Granddad's land
Look into a welding or farm machinery ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody can complain they weren't told. I'd also say the company owes the older crews something for their years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd mostly carry on. Robots by 2039, I'd be 40, and by then the cattle and the land could be a real living. I'd probably end up a farmer who used to be a lineman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, finish the farmhouse, grow the herd. I'd keep my savings safe in the bank, not in shares. And I'd wait and see how the robots actually go on city lines before I believed any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there but it's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes. For the young lads starting now, no. They'd only get ten or twelve years out of the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say work hard and the work will be there, and in this picture I'm not sure he'd be right. He believed that his whole life. That's hard to say.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning.
I'd say the company **owes older crews** something for their years.
think: I'd **mostly carry on**, since robots arrive when I'm forty.
I'd likely become a **farmer** who used to be a lineman.
do: Keep working, **finish the farmhouse** and grow the herd.
Keep savings **in the bank**, not in shares.
Wait to see how **robots on city lines** really perform.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the worry present but far off.
S4.quote: My dad would say work hard and the work will be there, and in this picture I'm not sure he'd be right.
fieldNote: Aaron sees ten years as enough for himself, but **not for apprentices**.
He'd **wait and see** robots tested on city lines before believing.
His father's **work ethic** is something he quietly doubts here.

steps.text: Watch how robots perform on city lines before changing anything
Grow the herd into a real second income
Keep working the Hollow Creek district

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It takes the depot and then the trade, and I'd have no time to finish the farmhouse. What would help is the company keeping small depots open and giving first pick of any new jobs to the people who've done the work for years, not to whoever's cheapest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. When the power goes out in calving season, farmers want a person they know, not a machine from the city. I don't think anyone building robots has thought about that.

headlineQuote: When the power goes out in calving season, farmers want a person they know, not a machine from the city.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old **rural lineworker** in the district his father worked for thirty-one years.
He has savings and **twelve acres** with a few cattle, inherited from his granddad.
He **never uses AI** and resents city head office changing how things are done.
He worries first about **losing his depot**, then his trade, most sharply in the fast picture.
His backup is **cattle and land**, and he prefers waiting to see over retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes the depot, then the trade, before the farmhouse is finished.
whatWouldHelp: First pick of new jobs for **long-serving crews**.
